claim: A mutation in the ciliary gene Inpp5e leads to a transient increase in direct neurogenesis in the developing cortex.
source: Here, we show that loss of Inpp5e function results in an increase in neuron formation at the expense of basal progenitor production in the E12.5 cortex
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased neuron formation and decreased basal progenitor production in E12.5 Inpp5e mutant embryos (Figures 1, 3).

claim: Loss of Inpp5e leads to an overproduction of layer V neurons in newborn mice.
source: Here, we show that loss of Inpp5e function results in an increase in neuron formation at the expense of basal progenitor production in the E12.5 cortex and in an overproduction of Ctip2+ layer V neurons in newborn mutants.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased proportion of Ctip2+ layer V neurons in E18.5 Inpp5e mutant embryos (Figure 4).

claim: Loss of Inpp5e affects ciliary structure in radial glial cells.
source: Loss of Inpp5e also affects ciliary structure coinciding with reduced Gli3 repressor levels.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data showing abnormal ciliary structures including unusual membranous structures and abnormal numbers of microtubule doublets (Figure 6).

claim: Loss of Inpp5e reduces Gli3 repressor levels in the developing cortex.
source: Loss of Inpp5e also affects ciliary structure coinciding with reduced Gli3 repressor levels.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing reduced Gli3R levels and Gli3R/Gli3FL ratio in E12.5 Inpp5e mutant dorsal telencephalon (Figure 7A-D).

claim: Genetically restoring Gli3 repressor rescues the decreased indirect neurogenesis in Inpp5e mutants.
source: Genetically restoring Gli3 repressor rescues the decreased indirect neurogenesis in Inpp5e mutants.
evidence: Supported by data showing that introducing Gli3Δ699 alleles into Inpp5e mutant background restores normal proportions of basal progenitors and neurons (Figures 7, 8).

claim: Primary cilia determine neuronal subtype composition of the cortex by controlling direct versus indirect neurogenesis.
source: Overall, our analyses reveal how primary cilia determine neuronal subtype composition of the cortex by controlling direct versus indirect neurogenesis.
evidence: Supported by data showing that ciliary gene mutations affect the balance between direct and indirect neurogenesis, leading to altered neuronal subtype composition.

claim: INPP5E is mutated in Joubert syndrome.
source: INPP5E is mutated in Joubert syndrome (JS) (Bielas et al., 2009; Jacoby et al., 2009), a ciliopathy characterized by cerebellar defects in which a subset of patients also shows malformations of the cerebral cortex including heterotopias, polymicrogyria and agenesis of the corpus callosum (Valente et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inpp5e encodes Inositol polyphosphate 5 phosphatase E, an enzyme localized in the ciliary membrane.
source: Inpp5e encodes Inositol polyphosphate 5 phosphatase E, an enzyme that is localized in the ciliary membrane and that hydrolyses the phosphatidylinositol polyphosphates PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3 (Bielas et al., 2009; Jacoby et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature describing the biochemical properties of Inpp5e.

claim: Inpp5e controls the inositol phosphate composition of the ciliary membrane.
source: In this way, it controls the inositol phosphate composition of the ciliary membrane and thereby regulates the activity of several signaling pathways and cilia stability (Bielas et al., 2009; Chávez et al., 2015; Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2015; Jacoby et al., 2009; Plotnikova et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Radial glial cells represent the major neural stem cell type in the developing murine cortex.
source: In the developing murine cortex, radial glial cells (RGCs) represent the major neural stem cell type.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cortical development.

claim: Radial glial cells reside in the ventricular zone and express Pax6.
source: Residing in the ventricular zone, they express Pax6 and undergo interkinetic nuclear migration dividing at the ventricular surface (Götz et al., 1998; Warren et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RGCs initially undergo symmetric proliferative divisions to produce two RGCs.
source: Initially, RGCs go through rounds of symmetric proliferative divisions to produce two RGCs increasing the progenitor pool but switch to asymmetric divisions at the beginning of cortical neurogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cortical development.

claim: RGCs generate neurons either directly or indirectly via the production of basal progenitors.
source: RGCs generate neurons in two ways, either directly or indirectly via the production of basal progenitors (BPs) that settle in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and express the Tbr2 transcription factor (Englund et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and established knowledge.

claim: Basal progenitors settle in the subventricular zone and express the Tbr2 transcription factor.
source: RGCs generate neurons in two ways, either directly or indirectly via the production of basal progenitors (BPs) that settle in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and express the Tbr2 transcription factor (Englund et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In the mouse, the majority of basal progenitors divide once to produce two neurons.
source: In the mouse, the majority of BPs divide once to produce two neurons, whereas the remainders undergo one additional round of symmetric proliferative division before differentiating into two neurons (Haubensak et al., 2004; Miyata, 2004; Noctor et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Basal progenitors increase neuron output per RGC.
source: In this way, BPs increase neuron output per RGC and have therefore been implicated in the evolutionary expansion of the mammalian cerebral cortex (Martínez-Cerdeño et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and logical inference.

claim: Basal progenitors have been implicated in the evolutionary expansion of the mammalian cerebral cortex.
source: In this way, BPs increase neuron output per RGC and have therefore been implicated in the evolutionary expansion of the mammalian cerebral cortex (Martínez-Cerdeño et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The balance between direct and indirect neurogenesis is an important factor in generating appropriate neuron numbers and types.
source: Thus, the balance between direct and indirect neurogenesis is an important factor in generating appropriate neuron numbers and types.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the described roles of direct and indirect neurogenesis.

claim: Mitotic spindle orientation contributes to control the generation of basal progenitors.
source: Mitotic spindle orientation (Postiglione et al., 2011) and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Gladwyn-Ng et al., 2018; Laguesse et al., 2015) are contributing factors to control the generation of basal progenitors.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Endoplasmic reticulum stress contributes to control the generation of basal progenitors.
source: Mitotic spindle orientation (Postiglione et al., 2011) and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Gladwyn-Ng et al., 2018; Laguesse et al., 2015) are contributing factors to control the generation of basal progenitors.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Levels of Slit/Robo and Notch/Delta signaling are evolutionarily conserved factors that determine the predominant mode of neurogenesis.
source: In addition, levels of Slit/Robo and Notch/Delta signaling were shown to be evolutionarily conserved factors that determine the predominant mode of neurogenesis (Cárdenas et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Feedback signals from postmitotic neurons control the fate of radial glial daughter cells.
source: Moreover, feedback signals from postmitotic neurons control the fate of radial glial daughter cells involving the release of Neurotrophin-3 and Fgf9 (Parthasarathy et al., 2014; Seuntjens et al., 2009) as well as the activation of a Notch-dependent signaling pathway (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The primary cilium is a signaling hub in embryogenesis and neural development.
source: Given the importance of cell-cell signaling, it is likely that the primary cilium, a signaling hub in embryogenesis in general and in neural development in particular (Valente et al., 2014), plays key roles in determining the balance between direct versus indirect neurogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The cilium is a subcellular protrusion that predominately emanates from the apical surface of RGCs projecting into the ventricular lumen.
source: The cilium is a subcellular protrusion that predominately emanates from the apical surface of RGCs projecting into the ventricular lumen.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ciliary structure and localization.

claim: Mouse mutants for ciliary genes often suffer from severe patterning defects in forebrain development.
source: The phenotypes of several mouse lines mutant for ciliary genes underline the importance of the primary cilium in forebrain development but these mutants often suffer from severe patterning defects (Ashique et al., 2009; Besse et al., 2011; Willaredt et al., 2008) which make elucidating ciliary roles in determining the lineage of cortical progenitors difficult.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Joubert syndrome is characterized by cerebellar defects.
source: INPP5E is mutated in Joubert syndrome (JS) (Bielas et al., 2009; Jacoby et al., 2009), a ciliopathy characterized by cerebellar defects in which a subset of patients also shows malformations of the cerebral cortex including heterotopias, polymicrogyria and agenesis of the corpus callosum (Valente et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A subset of Joubert syndrome patients shows malformations of the cerebral cortex including heterotopias, polymicrogyria and agenesis of the corpus callosum.
source: INPP5E is mutated in Joubert syndrome (JS) (Bielas et al., 2009; Jacoby et al., 2009), a ciliopathy characterized by cerebellar defects in which a subset of patients also shows malformations of the cerebral cortex including heterotopias, polymicrogyria and agenesis of the corpus callosum (Valente et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos show mild telencephalic patterning defects.
source: Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos show mild telencephalic patterning defects
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data showing defects at the pallial/subpallial boundary and hippocampal development (Figure 1—figure supplements 1-3).

claim: E12.5 control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos show no obvious effect on the expression of dorsal and ventral telencephalic markers at the corticoseptal boundary.
source: In situ hybridization and immunofluorescence analyses of E12.5 control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos revealed no obvious effect on the expression of dorsal and ventral telencephalic markers at the corticoseptal boundary (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-F.

claim: The pallial/subpallial boundary is not well defined in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos with scattered Pax6+ and Dlx2 expressing cells on the wrong side of the boundary.
source: In contrast, the pallial/subpallial boundary was not well defined with a few scattered Pax6+ and Dlx2 expressing cells on the wrong side of the boundary, that is in the subpallium and pallium, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-L.

claim: The hippocampal anlage appears smaller and disorganized in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos with low level and diffuse expression of cortical hem markers.
source: Moreover, the hippocampal anlage appeared smaller and disorganized with low level and diffuse expression of cortical hem markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), consistent with known roles of Wnt/β-catenin and Bmp signaling in hippocampal development (Galceran et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to published literature.

claim: Progenitors in the neocortical ventricular zone of Inpp5e mutant mice express the progenitor markers Emx1, Lhx2, Pax6 and Ngn2.
source: In contrast, progenitors in the neocortical ventricular zone of Inpp5e mutant mice expressed the progenitor markers Emx1, Lhx2, Pax6 and Ngn2, though the levels of Pax6 protein expression appeared reduced in the medial neocortex suggestive of a steeper lateral to medial Pax6 expression gradient in mutant embryos.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Pax6 protein expression levels appear reduced in the medial neocortex of Inpp5e mutants.
source: In contrast, progenitors in the neocortical ventricular zone of Inpp5e mutant mice expressed the progenitor markers Emx1, Lhx2, Pax6 and Ngn2, though the levels of Pax6 protein expression appeared reduced in the medial neocortex suggestive of a steeper lateral to medial Pax6 expression gradient in mutant embryos.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos show an area in the very caudal/dorsal telencephalon where the neocortex is folded.
source: These expression patterns were maintained in E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos but revealed an area in the very caudal/dorsal telencephalon where the neocortex was folded (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The proportion of RGCs is not different between control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos at E12.5 in both medial and lateral neocortex.
source: Double immunofluorescence for PCNA which labels all progenitor cells (Hall et al., 1990) and the radial glial marker Pax6 did not reveal differences in the proportions of RGCs at both medial and lateral levels (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: The proportion of Tbr2+ basal progenitors is reduced in the lateral but not medial neocortex of E12.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: In contrast, the proportion of Tbr2+ basal progenitors was reduced laterally but not medially (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The proportion of Tbr1+ neurons is increased in the lateral neocortex of E12.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This decrease coincided with an increase in Tbr1+ neurons specifically in the lateral neocortex (Figure 1I–L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I-L.

claim: There is no significant difference in the proportion of Pax6+ RGCs in E14.5 control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This analysis revealed no significant differences in the proportion of Pax6+ RGCs (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: There is no alteration in the proportion of Tbr2+ basal progenitors in the lateral neocortex of E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Similarly, there was no alteration in the proportion of Tbr2+ basal progenitors in lateral neocortex; however, their proportion was reduced medially (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: The proportion of Tbr2+ basal progenitors is reduced in the medial neocortex of E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Similarly, there was no alteration in the proportion of Tbr2+ basal progenitors in lateral neocortex; however, their proportion was reduced medially (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: The proportion of Tbr1+Ctip2+ neurons is not significantly altered in E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Quantifying these subpopulations showed no effect on the formation of Tbr1+ Ctip2+ neurons in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I-L.

claim: The proportion of Tbr1-Ctip2+ neurons is reduced medially but increased in the lateral neocortex of E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: In contrast, the proportion of Tbr1- Ctip2+ neurons was reduced medially but increased in the lateral neocortex (Figure 2I–N).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I-N.

claim: Few apoptotic cells are found in the control and mutant cortex.
source: To address the defective cellular processes underlying these neurogenesis defects in Inpp5e mutants, we first investigated programmed cell death and found few apoptotic cells in the control and mutant cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Cleaved Caspase 3 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are no statistically significant differences in proliferation rates in the E12.5 and E14.5 lateral neocortex of control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This analysis revealed no statistically significant differences in the E12.5 and E14.5 lateral neocortex of control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
evidence: Supported by pHH3/PCNA double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The proportion of mitotic apical and basal progenitors is reduced in the E12.5 medial neocortex of Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: The proportion of mitotic apical and basal progenitors, however, was reduced in the E12.5 medial neocortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by pHH3/PCNA double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There are no statistically significant changes in S phase length and total cell cycle length in RGCs of Inpp5e mutants.
source: To investigate the possibility of altered cell cycle kinetics, we used a BrdU/IdU double labeling strategy (Martynoga et al., 2005; Nowakowski et al., 1989) to determine S phase length and total cell cycle length in RGCs and found no statistically significant changes in these parameters (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by BrdU/IdU double labeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The proportion of Tbr1+ neurons increases while the Tbr2+ proportion decreases in the lateral neocortex of Inpp5e mutants in a 24 hr BrdU labeling experiment.
source: This analysis showed that the proportion of Tbr1+ neurons compared to the total number of BrdU+ cells increased while the Tbr2+ proportion decreased in Inpp5e mutants (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by BrdU/Tbr1/Tbr2 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Direct neurogenesis becomes more prevalent in Inpp5eΔ/Δ RGCs.
source: Since the cell cycle of basal progenitors is longer than 24 hr (Arai et al., 2011), the 24 hr interval used in our cell cycle exit experiment was too short for newly formed basal progenitors to undergo one additional round of the cell cycle and as the BrdU label would have been diluted with a further round of division, this analysis supports our hypothesis that direct neurogenesis became more prevalent in Inpp5eΔ/ΔRGCs.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data and logical inference based on cell cycle length of basal progenitors.

claim: The mutant Inpp5eΔ/Δ brain lacks obvious olfactory bulbs.
source: The mutant lacked obvious olfactory bulbs, as revealed by whole mounts of control and mutant brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by whole mount brain images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most of the mutant cortex is thinner except for the rostrolateral level in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This analysis showed that most of the mutant cortex was thinner except for the rostrolateral level (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and cortical thickness measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hippocampus is malformed with a smaller dentate gyrus in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: In addition, the hippocampus was malformed with a smaller dentate gyrus.
evidence: Supported by DAPI staining and hippocampal marker expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: Hippocampal structures are present but severely reduced in size and disorganized in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Investigating the expression of markers characteristic of the entire hippocampus (Nrp2; Galceran et al., 2000), the CA1 field (Scip1; Frantz et al., 1994) and the dentate gyrus (Prox1; Oliver et al., 1993) showed that these hippocampal structures were present but were severely reduced in size and disorganized in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The corpus callosum is smaller in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: In addition, the corpus callosum, the major axon tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, was smaller. We confirmed this effect by staining callosal axons and surrounding glial cells that guide these axons to the contralateral hemisphere with L1 and GFAP, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by L1 and GFAP immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tbr1+, Ctip2+ and Satb2+ neurons occupy their correct relative laminar positions in Inpp5e mutants.
source: Inspecting these immunostainings at low magnification showed that Tbr1+, Ctip2+ and Satb2+ neurons occupied their correct relative laminar positions in Inpp5e mutants (Figure 4A–F) except for neuronal heterotopias which were present in all mutant brains, although their number and position varied (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: Neuronal heterotopias are present in all Inpp5e mutant brains, although their number and position vary.
source: Inspecting these immunostainings at low magnification showed that Tbr1+, Ctip2+ and Satb2+ neurons occupied their correct relative laminar positions in Inpp5e mutants (Figure 4A–F) except for neuronal heterotopias which were present in all mutant brains, although their number and position varied (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a medial shift in the position of the rhinal fissure in Inpp5e mutants.
source: These immunostainings also revealed a medial shift in the position of the rhinal fissure, a sulcus that is conserved across mammalian species and separates neocortex from the paleocortical piriform cortex (Ariens-Kapers et al., 1936).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The medial shift of the rhinal fissure suggests a dramatic expansion of the Inpp5e mutant piriform cortex at the expense of neocortex at caudal most levels.
source: This shift was more marked caudally and suggests a dramatic expansion of the Inpp5e mutant piriform cortex at the expense of neocortex at caudal most levels (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D-F and logical inference.

claim: The proportion of Tbr1+ neurons is reduced in the rostrolateral neocortex of E18.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: In the rostrolateral neocortex, we found the proportion of Tbr1+ neurons to be reduced (Figure 4G,H,M).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G, H, M.

claim: The proportion of Ctip2+ layer V neurons is increased in the rostrolateral neocortex of E18.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This reduction coincided with an increased proportion of Ctip2+ layer V neurons (Figure 4I,J,N) while the Satb2 population was unchanged (Figure 4K,L,O).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I, J, N.

claim: The Satb2+ population is unchanged in the rostrolateral neocortex of E18.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This reduction coincided with an increased proportion of Ctip2+ layer V neurons (Figure 4I,J,N) while the Satb2 population was unchanged (Figure 4K,L,O).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4K, L, O.

claim: The rostromedial neocortex does not show any differences in neuronal proportions in E18.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: In contrast, the rostromedial neocortex did not show any differences (Figure 4P–X).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4P-X.

claim: E12.5 Tctn2Δ/Δ mutant embryos show an increased proportion of Tbr1+ projection neurons in the dorsolateral telencephalon.
source: Interestingly, E12.5 Tctn2Δ/Δ mutant embryos (Reiter and Skarnes, 2006) also showed an increased proportion of Tbr1+ projection neurons and a concomitant decrease in Tbr2+ basal progenitors in the dorsolateral telencephalon (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5.

claim: E12.5 Tctn2Δ/Δ mutant embryos show a decrease in Tbr2+ basal progenitors in the dorsolateral telencephalon.
source: Interestingly, E12.5 Tctn2Δ/Δ mutant embryos (Reiter and Skarnes, 2006) also showed an increased proportion of Tbr1+ projection neurons and a concomitant decrease in Tbr2+ basal progenitors in the dorsolateral telencephalon (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is no major difference in the number or apical localization of cilia in control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ neuroepithelial cells in the E12.5 telencephalon.
source: We found no major difference in the number or the apical localization of cilia in control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ neuroepithelial cells in the E12.5 telencephalon (Figure 6A,B) or diencephalon (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by Arl13b and γ-Tubulin immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: Scanning electron microscopy reveals the presence of abnormal cilia in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos having a spherical shape or aberrant lateral buddings.
source: However, SEM also revealed the presence of abnormal cilia in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos having a spherical shape (arrows in D and E) or aberrant lateral buddings (arrowheads in D and E).
evidence: Supported by scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 6D, E.

claim: Abnormal cilia in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos lack an axoneme or show unusual membranous structures.
source: In addition to cilia with normal morphology, abnormal cilia were identified in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos thanks to the presence of a basal body apparently correctly docked to the apical membrane. Abnormal cilia lacked an axoneme (I, J, L) or showed unusual membranous structures, such as budding (G, K) or internal (I, K, L) vesicles (arrows) or undulating peripheral membranes (I).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 6G-L.

claim: Transverse sections of primary cilia in Inpp5eΔ/Δ brains reveal the presence of normal axonemes and abnormal axonemes containing a lower number of microtubule doublets.
source: However, transverse section of primary cilia in Inpp5eΔ/Δ brains revealed the presence of normal axonemes composed of nine correctly organized doublets of microtubules on some radial glial cells (O), while others harbored an abnormal axoneme containing a lower number of microtubule doublets (P).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 6O, P.

claim: There is an increase in abnormal cilia in Inpp5eΔ/Δ compared to control embryos.
source: To quantify these ciliary defects, we counted the number of normal versus abnormal cilia on TEM images obtained from control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos, and found an increase in abnormal cilia in Inpp5eΔ/Δ compared to control embryos (Figure 6R).
evidence: Supported by quantification of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6R.

claim: A significant number of abnormal primary cilia are found at the apical end of E12.5 RGCs in the forebrain of Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Taken together, a significant number of abnormal primary cilia were found at the apical end of E12.5 RGCs in the forebrain of Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ciliary abnormalities in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos are consistent with a role of Inpp5e in maintaining cilia stability.
source: These abnormalities are consistent with a role of Inpp5e in maintaining cilia stability (Jacoby et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data and citation to published literature.

claim: Primary cilia control the proteolytic cleavage of full-length Gli3 into the Gli3 repressor form in the absence of Shh.
source: Primary cilia play a crucial role in Shh signaling by controlling the proteolytic cleavage of full-length Gli3 (Gli3FL) into the Gli3 repressor form (Gli3R) in the absence of Shh and by converting Gli3FL into the transcriptional activator Gli3A in the presence of Shh.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Shh signaling and ciliary function.

claim: Primary cilia convert Gli3FL into the transcriptional activator Gli3A in the presence of Shh.
source: Primary cilia play a crucial role in Shh signaling by controlling the proteolytic cleavage of full-length Gli3 (Gli3FL) into the Gli3 repressor form (Gli3R) in the absence of Shh and by converting Gli3FL into the transcriptional activator Gli3A in the presence of Shh.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Shh signaling and ciliary function.

claim: The dorsal telencephalon predominately forms Gli3R.
source: Moreover, the dorsal telencephalon predominately forms Gli3R (Fotaki et al., 2006) and mice that can only produce Gli3R have no obvious defect in cortical development (Besse et al., 2011; Bose, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice that can only produce Gli3R have no obvious defect in cortical development.
source: Moreover, the dorsal telencephalon predominately forms Gli3R (Fotaki et al., 2006) and mice that can only produce Gli3R have no obvious defect in cortical development (Besse et al., 2011; Bose, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gli3 has a prominent role in RGCs controlling the switch from symmetric proliferative to asymmetric neurogenic cell division.
source: In addition, we recently showed that Gli3 has a prominent role in RGCs controlling the switch from symmetric proliferative to asymmetric neurogenic cell division (Hasenpusch-Theil et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Gli3 mRNA expression is slightly reduced but the overall expression pattern in the telencephalon remains unaffected in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: In situ hybridization showed that Gli3 mRNA expression might be slightly reduced but the overall expression pattern in the telencephalon remains unaffected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no change in the levels of Gli3FL in the E12.5 dorsal telencephalon of Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This analysis revealed no change in the levels of Gli3FL but a significant decrease inGli3R which resulted in a reduced Gli3R to Gli3FL ratio in the mutant (Figure 7A–D) suggesting that the Inpp5e mutation affects Gli3 processing.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: There is a significant decrease in Gli3R levels in the E12.5 dorsal telencephalon of Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This analysis revealed no change in the levels of Gli3FL but a significant decrease inGli3R which resulted in a reduced Gli3R to Gli3FL ratio in the mutant (Figure 7A–D) suggesting that the Inpp5e mutation affects Gli3 processing.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: The Gli3R to Gli3FL ratio is reduced in the E12.5 dorsal telencephalon of Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This analysis revealed no change in the levels of Gli3FL but a significant decrease inGli3R which resulted in a reduced Gli3R to Gli3FL ratio in the mutant (Figure 7A–D) suggesting that the Inpp5e mutation affects Gli3 processing.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: The Inpp5e mutation affects Gli3 processing.
source: This analysis revealed no change in the levels of Gli3FL but a significant decrease inGli3R which resulted in a reduced Gli3R to Gli3FL ratio in the mutant (Figure 7A–D) suggesting that the Inpp5e mutation affects Gli3 processing.
evidence: Supported by western blot data and logical inference.

claim: Eye formation is restored in Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos.
source: Overall inspection of Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos revealed restored eye formation, whereas Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos either completely lacked eyes or showed microphthalmia (Jacoby et al., 2009; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by images of embryo heads shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos either completely lack eyes or show microphthalmia.
source: Overall inspection of Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos revealed restored eye formation, whereas Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos either completely lacked eyes or showed microphthalmia (Jacoby et al., 2009; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by images of embryo heads shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and citation to published literature.

claim: The overall morphology of the telencephalon is much improved in Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos compared to Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Moreover, the overall morphology of the telencephalon is much improved in Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos as compared to Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The corpus callosum has a thickness indistinguishable from that of control embryos in E18.5 Inpp5eΔ/ΔGli3Δ699/+ mutants.
source: In E18.5 Inpp5eΔ/ΔGli3Δ699/+ mutants, the corpus callosum has a thickness indistinguishable from that of control embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by L1 and GFAP immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The neocortex lacks the undulations of the VZ present in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos in E12.5 and E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos.
source: In E12.5 and E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos, the neocortex lacks the undulations of the VZ present in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos (data not shown) and the morphology of the hippocampal anlage is more akin to that in wild-type embryos but it is still smaller and less bulged (Figure 7E,G,I).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The morphology of the hippocampal anlage is more akin to that in wild-type embryos but it is still smaller and less bulged in Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos.
source: In E12.5 and E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos, the neocortex lacks the undulations of the VZ present in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos (data not shown) and the morphology of the hippocampal anlage is more akin to that in wild-type embryos but it is still smaller and less bulged (Figure 7E,G,I).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E, G, I.

claim: There is no statistically significant difference in the proportions of basal progenitors and Tbr1+ neurons between control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos at E12.5 in the lateral neocortex.
source: While these changes were still present in Inpp5eΔ/Δ littermate embryos, there was no statistically significant difference between control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos (Figure 7E–L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E-L.

claim: The neurogenesis phenotype of E12.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ mutants is rescued by a single copy of the Gli3Δ699 allele.
source: This finding indicates that the neurogenesis phenotype of E12.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ mutants is rescued by a single copy of the Gli3Δ699 allele.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7 and statistical analysis.

claim: The proportion of Tbr1+Ctip2+ neurons is not affected in the medial neocortex of E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos.
source: The proportion of Tbr1+Ctip2+ neurons was not affected in the medial neocortex of E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The proportion of Tbr1-Ctip2+ neurons is reduced in the medial neocortex of E14.5 Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos as in Inpp5eΔ/Δ mutants.
source: In contrast, the proportion of Tbr1-Ctip2+ neurons was reduced as in Inpp5eΔ/Δ mutants (Figure 8A,C,E,I,J).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A, C, E, I, J.

claim: The proportion of basal progenitors in the medial Inpp5eΔ/ΔGli3Δ699/+ neocortex is slightly improved compared to Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos but significantly smaller than in control embryos.
source: Similarly, the proportions of basal progenitors in the medial Inpp5eΔ/ΔGli3Δ699/+ neocortex was slightly improved compared to Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos but significantly smaller than in control embryos (Figure 8B,D,F,K).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B, D, F, K.

claim: The morphology of the dorsal telencephalon including the hippocampal formation is indistinguishable between control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/Δ699 embryos.
source: Interestingly, the morphology of the dorsal telencephalon including the hippocampal formation was indistinguishable between control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/Δ699 embryos (Figure 8A,B,G,H) and the formation of Tbr1-Ctip2+ neurons and Tbr2+ basal progenitors were not affected (Figure 8G,H,J,K).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A, B, G, H.

claim: The formation of Tbr1-Ctip2+ neurons and Tbr2+ basal progenitors is not affected in Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/Δ699 embryos.
source: Interestingly, the morphology of the dorsal telencephalon including the hippocampal formation was indistinguishable between control and Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/Δ699 embryos (Figure 8A,B,G,H) and the formation of Tbr1-Ctip2+ neurons and Tbr2+ basal progenitors were not affected (Figure 8G,H,J,K).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8G, H, J, K.

claim: Re-introducing a single copy of the Gli3R allele into the Inpp5e mutant background leads to a partial rescue of cortical neurogenesis.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that re-introducing a single copy of the Gli3R allele into the Inpp5e mutant background leads to a partial rescue of cortical neurogenesis in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos, whereas two copies are required for a full rescue.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Two copies of the Gli3R allele are required for a full rescue of cortical neurogenesis in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that re-introducing a single copy of the Gli3R allele into the Inpp5e mutant background leads to a partial rescue of cortical neurogenesis in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos, whereas two copies are required for a full rescue.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The Inpp5e mutation results in an increase in neuron formation at the expense of basal progenitor production in the lateral neocortex.
source: In the E12.5 Inpp5e and Tctn2 mouse mutants, we identified an increased formation of neurons in the lateral neocortex. Based on our cell cycle exit experiment, additional neurons are formed from RGCs at the expense of basal progenitors.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1, 3, and 5.

claim: The Inpp5e mutation causes RGCs to preferentially produce neurons directly.
source: We therefore conclude that the Inpp5e mutation caused RGCs to preferentially produce neurons directly.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data and logical inference.

claim: Neurogenesis defects only become obvious at E14.5 in the medial neocortex of Inpp5e mutants.
source: Moreover, neurogenesis defects only became obvious at E14.5 in the medial neocortex.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The delay in neurogenesis defects in the medial neocortex might reflect the neurogenic gradient in the neocortex or might be related to specific gene expression changes such as reduced Pax6 expression.
source: This delay might reflect the neurogenic gradient in the neocortex or might be related to specific gene expression changes such as reduced Pax6 expression in medial neocortical progenitors.
evidence: Based on speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The increase in direct neurogenesis led to an increased proportion of Ctip2+ deep layer V neurons in the E18.5 neocortex but did not coincide with a reduced proportion of upper layer neurons.
source: Interestingly, the increase in direct neurogenesis led to an increased proportion of Ctip2+ deep layer V neurons in the E18.5 neocortex but did not coincide with a reduced proportion of upper layer neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neurons born at E12.5 initially express both Ctip2 and Tbr1 and later down-regulate Ctip2.
source: First, neurons born at E12.5 initially express both Ctip2 and Tbr1 (Figure 7) and later down-regulate Ctip2.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7 and established knowledge.

claim: Inpp5e could affect the signaling that controls Ctip2 downregulation.
source: Inpp5e could therefore affect the signaling that controls this downregulation.
evidence: Based on speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The proportions of basal progenitors and neurons are normalized in E14.5 Inpp5e mutants.
source: Secondly, the proportions of basal progenitors and neurons were normalized in E14.5 mutants.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Basal progenitors are a main source of upper layer neurons.
source: Since basal progenitors are a main source of upper layer neurons (Arnold et al., 2008; Vasistha et al., 2015), this normalization would account for the sufficient numbers of Satb2+ upper layer neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Newly formed projection neurons signal back to RGCs via Jag1, Fgf9 and Neurotrophin 3 to control the sequential production of deep and upper layer neurons and of glia.
source: Newly formed projection neurons signal back to RGCs via Jag1, Fgf9 and Neurotrophin 3 (Parthasarathy et al., 2014; Seuntjens et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2016) to control the sequential production of deep and upper layer neurons and of glia (Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inpp5e might affect feedback signals from neurons by controlling cilia stability and/or levels of PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: Inpp5e might affect these signals by controlling cilia stability and/or levels of PI(3,4,5)P3 (Bielas et al., 2009; Jacoby et al., 2009) that acts as a second messenger in receptor tyrosine kinase signaling.
evidence: Based on speculation about possible mechanisms and citations to published literature.

claim: Inpp5e has a novel, spatially and temporally restricted role in controlling the decision between direct and indirect neurogenesis.
source: Regardless of the exact mechanism, our findings suggest a novel, spatially and temporally restricted role for Inpp5e in controlling the decision between direct and indirect neurogenesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and logical inference.

claim: The function of Inpp5e in controlling direct versus indirect neurogenesis differs from those described for other cilia mutants.
source: This function differs from those described for other cilia mutants. Conditional inactivation of Ift88 and Kif3a leads to a larger cortex (Foerster et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2012) with a modest increase in BP production in the absence of a delay in neurogenesis (Foerster et al., 2017) while Rpgrip1l mutants have reduced numbers of both basal progenitors and neurons (Postel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature describing phenotypes of other cilia mutants.

claim: Conditional inactivation of Ift88 and Kif3a leads to a larger cortex with a modest increase in BP production in the absence of a delay in neurogenesis.
source: Conditional inactivation of Ift88 and Kif3a leads to a larger cortex (Foerster et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2012) with a modest increase in BP production in the absence of a delay in neurogenesis (Foerster et al., 2017) while Rpgrip1l mutants have reduced numbers of both basal progenitors and neurons (Postel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Rpgrip1l mutants have reduced numbers of both basal progenitors and neurons.
source: Conditional inactivation of Ift88 and Kif3a leads to a larger cortex (Foerster et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2012) with a modest increase in BP production in the absence of a delay in neurogenesis (Foerster et al., 2017) while Rpgrip1l mutants have reduced numbers of both basal progenitors and neurons (Postel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cilia play multiple and varied roles in cortical development.
source: These findings highlight the multiple and varied roles cilia play in cortical development.
evidence: Based on inference from the diverse phenotypes of different cilia mutants.

claim: The Inpp5e mutation does not lead to an up-regulation of Shh signaling in the dorsal telencephalon.
source: While the Inpp5e mutation does not lead to an up-regulation of Shh signaling in the dorsal telencephalon (Magnani et al., 2015), re-introducing a single or two copies of Gli3R in an Inpp5e mutant background partially and fully restores the neurogenesis defects, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Re-introducing a single or two copies of Gli3R in an Inpp5e mutant background partially and fully restores the neurogenesis defects, respectively.
source: While the Inpp5e mutation does not lead to an up-regulation of Shh signaling in the dorsal telencephalon (Magnani et al., 2015), re-introducing a single or two copies of Gli3R in an Inpp5e mutant background partially and fully restores the neurogenesis defects, respectively.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Reduced levels of Gli3R rather than the reduction in the Gli3R/Gli3FL ratio are responsible for the prevalence of direct neurogenesis in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: This rescue indicates that reduced levels of Gli3R rather than the reduction in the Gli3R/Gli3FL ratio are responsible for the prevalence of direct neurogenesis in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
evidence: Based on inference from the rescue experiments.

claim: Gli3Δ699/Δ699 embryos that cannot produce Gli3FL and Gli3A show no obvious phenotype in cortical development.
source: This idea is consistent with the findings that (i) Gli3Δ699/Δ699 embryos that cannot produce Gli3FL and Gli3A show no obvious phenotype in cortical development (Besse et al., 2011; Bose, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dorsal telencephalic patterning defects in Gli3Xt/Xt mutants are not rescued in Shh-/-/Gli3XtXt double mutants.
source: (ii) dorsal telencephalic patterning defects in Gli3Xt/Xt mutants are not rescued in Shh-/-/Gli3XtXt double mutants (Rallu et al., 2002; Rash and Grove, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Shh promotes the generation of olfactory bulb interneurons and cortical oligodendrocytes and neurogenesis in the subventricular zone by reducing Gli3R rather than by promoting Gli activator function.
source: (iii) Shh promotes the generation of olfactory bulb interneurons and cortical oligodendrocytes and neurogenesis in the subventricular zone by reducing Gli3R rather than by promoting Gli activator function (Petrova et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is a dramatic rescue of eye development in Inpp5eΔ/Δ;Gli3Δ699/+ embryos.
source: In addition, there is also a dramatic rescue of eye development and the rescue also extends to other malformations of the Inpp5eΔ/Δ forebrain, including the corpus callosum, the hippocampus and the expansion of the piriform cortex
evidence: Supported by images and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The rescue of Inpp5e mutant phenotypes by Gli3R extends to other malformations including the corpus callosum, the hippocampus and the expansion of the piriform cortex.
source: In addition, there is also a dramatic rescue of eye development and the rescue also extends to other malformations of the Inpp5eΔ/Δ forebrain, including the corpus callosum, the hippocampus and the expansion of the piriform cortex, structures that are also affected in Gli3 null and hypomorphic mutants (Amaniti et al., 2015; Johnson, 1967; Magnani et al., 2014; Theil et al., 1999; Wiegering et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and citations to published literature.

claim: The corpus callosum, hippocampus and piriform cortex are affected in Gli3 null and hypomorphic mutants.
source: structures that are also affected in Gli3 null and hypomorphic mutants (Amaniti et al., 2015; Johnson, 1967; Magnani et al., 2014; Theil et al., 1999; Wiegering et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inpp5e and the primary cilium control key processes in cortical development by regulating the formation of Gli3R.
source: Taken together, these findings support the idea that Inpp5e and the primary cilium control key processes in cortical development by regulating the formation of Gli3R.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and logical inference.

claim: The Inpp5e mutation impacts on Gli3 processing through effects on cilia stability.
source: Our analyses support several mutually non-exclusive mechanisms how the Inpp5e mutation impacts on Gli3 processing. First, our electron microscopy study revealed severe structural abnormalities in large proportions of cilia.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data and logical inference.

claim: The Inpp5e phosphatase hydrolyses PI(3,4,5)P3, which is essential for the effective activation of the serine threonine kinase Akt.
source: The Inpp5e phosphatase hydrolyses PI(3,4,5)P3, which is essential for the effective activation of the serine threonine kinase Akt (Kisseleva et al., 2002; Plotnikova et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Following PI(3,4,5)P3 binding, Akt translocates to the membrane and becomes phosphorylated at T308 by Pdk1 and at S473 by mTORC2.
source: Following PI(3,4,5)P3 binding, Akt translocates to the membrane and becomes phosphorylated at T308 by phosphoinositide-dependent kinase-1 (Pdk1) and at S473 by mammalian target of rapamycin complex (mTORC2) (Yu and Cui, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Western blot analysis reveals elevated pAktS473 levels in Inpp5e mutants.
source: Consistent with the loss of Inpp5e function and a resulting increase in PI(3,4,5)P3, western blot analysis revealed elevated pAktS473 levels (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by western blot data.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of Akt at S473 has been implicated in inhibiting cilia assembly and promoting cilia disassembly.
source: Increased phosphorylation at this site has been implicated in inhibiting cilia assembly and promoting cilia disassembly (Mao et al., 2019) and could hence explain the structural defects of RGC Inpp5eΔ/Δ cilia.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and logical inference.

claim: Inpp5e is required for transition zone molecular organization.
source: Secondly, Inpp5e could control Gli3 processing through its effect on the transition zone (TZ). It is required for TZ molecular organization (Dyson et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: PI(4,5)P2, a substrate of Inpp5e, plays a role in transition zone maturation in Drosophila.
source: and its substrate PI(4,5)P2 plays a role in TZ maturation in Drosophila (Gupta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A mouse mutant for the TZ protein Tctn2 phenocopies the Inpp5eΔ/Δ neurogenesis defect.
source: This model is further supported by our finding that a mouse mutant for the TZ protein Tctn2 phenocopies the Inpp5eΔ/Δ neurogenesis defect.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Several mouse mutants defective for TZ proteins are required for Inpp5e localization to cilia and show microphthalmia.
source: In turn, several mouse mutants defective for TZ proteins are required for Inpp5e localization to cilia and show microphthalmia (Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2011; Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2015; Sang et al., 2011; Yee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tctn proteins are required for Gli3 processing.
source: Tctn proteins are also required for Gli3 processing (Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2011; Sang et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The TZ protein Rpgrip1l controls the activity of the proteasome at the basal body responsible for proteolytic cleavage of Gli3.
source: and the TZ protein Rpgrip1l controls the activity of the proteasome at the basal body responsible for proteolytic cleavage of Gli3 (Gerhardt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Inpp5e mutation might affect the ability of RGCs to switch to indirect neurogenesis through defects in cilia stability and/or the integrity of the ciliary transition zone.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that Inpp5e mutation might affect the ability of RGCs to switch to indirect neurogenesis through defects in cilia stability and/or the integrity of the ciliary transition zone (Figure 9).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and published literature.

claim: The Inpp5e mouse mutant recapitulates cortical abnormalities in Joubert syndrome patients.
source: Thus, the Inpp5eΔ/Δ mutant recapitulates cortical abnormalities in JS patients and starts to help unravelling the pathomechanisms underlying these defects.
evidence: Supported by comparison of mouse mutant phenotypes with human patient phenotypes.

claim: In the caudal telencephalon, the otherwise lissencephalic cortex forms folds reminiscent of the polymicrogyria in Joubert syndrome patients.
source: In the caudal telencephalon, the otherwise lissencephalic cortex formed folds reminiscent of the polymicrogyria in JS patients.
evidence: Supported by histological data and comparison with human patient phenotypes.

claim: The Inpp5e mutant forms leptomeningeal heterotopias with 100% penetrance, but their number and location vary.
source: In addition, the mutant formed leptomeningeal heterotopias with 100% penetrance, but their number and location varied.
evidence: Supported by histological data.

claim: Mutations in ciliary genes were previously associated with heterotopia formation in humans and mice.
source: Mutations in ciliary genes were previously associated with heterotopia formation in humans and mice (Magnani et al., 2015; Uzquiano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice carrying mutations in the Eml1 gene show subcortical heterotopias due to a mispositioning of RGCs and impaired primary cilia formation.
source: Mice carrying mutations in the Eml1 gene encoding a microtubule-associated protein show subcortical heterotopias due to a mispositioning of RGCs and impaired primary cilia formation (Uzquiano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The corpus callosum is thinner but callosal axons project to the contralateral cerebral hemisphere in Inpp5e mutants.
source: Finally, the corpus callosum is thinner but callosal axons project to the contralateral cerebral hemisphere in Inpp5e mutants.
evidence: Supported by L1 and GFAP immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Inpp5e mutant corpus callosum phenotype is milder compared to that of other mouse mutants with altered cilia that show complete agenesis of the corpus callosum with callosal axons forming Probst bundles.
source: This phenotype is milder compared to that of other mouse mutants with altered cilia that show complete agenesis of the corpus callosum with callosal axons forming Probst bundles (Benadiba et al., 2012; Laclef et al., 2015; Putoux et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by comparison with published literature on other cilia mutants.

claim: The corticoseptal boundary is not obviously affected in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
source: Unlike these other ciliary mutants, the corticoseptal boundary which plays a crucial role in positioning guidepost cells that control midline crossing of callosal axons (Magnani et al., 2014) is not obviously affected in Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The thinner corpus callosum in Inpp5e mutants is likely to be the result of reduced size of the caudal neocortex.
source: Instead, the thinner corpus callosum is likely to be the result of reduced size of the caudal neocortex.
evidence: Based on inference from histological data.

claim: Re-introducing Gli3R into the cilia mutant background restores callosal development in both Inpp5e mutants and other ciliary mutants.
source: Despite these differences, however, re-introducing Gli3R into the cilia mutant background restores callosal development in both groups of mutants suggesting that cilia control two independent steps in corpus callosum formation by regulating Gli3 processing.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and comparison with published literature.

claim: Cilia control two independent steps in corpus callosum formation by regulating Gli3 processing.
source: Despite these differences, however, re-introducing Gli3R into the cilia mutant background restores callosal development in both groups of mutants suggesting that cilia control two independent steps in corpus callosum formation by regulating Gli3 processing.
evidence: Based on inference from rescue experiments in different mutant backgrounds.

claim: Inpp5eΔ/Δ newborn pups die perinatally.
source: Since Inpp5eΔ/Δ newborn pups die perinatally (Bielas et al., 2009), we focused our analysis on E18.5 embryos.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Exencephalic Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos make up ca. 25% of homozygous mutant embryos.
source: Inpp5eΔ/+ mice were interbred to generate Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos; exencephalic Inpp5eΔ/Δ embryos which made up ca. 25% of homozygous mutant embryos were excluded from the analyses.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.
